C0.quote: each of n agents (voters) may nominate one candidate
C0.note: Committee sequence election from agents' nominations; computational complexity of a voting-type procedure.

C1.quote: We analyze the parameterized complexity of finding such committees
C1.note: All main results are hardness, FPT algorithms and kernelization.

C2.1.quote: a sequence of nomination profiles U = (u1 , . . . , uτ )

C2.2.note: Each agent nominates at most one candidate per level (single-candidate nomination). Approval-like but not a general approval set.

C2.3.note: Agents' nominations are the only attitude; a utility function is mentioned only in the outlook and the proof notation, and is defined as the nomination.

C2.4.quote: every agent may nominate one candidate for the committee
C2.4.note: Input is only something submitted; no held attitude is referred to. Text such as 'Preferences indicating the favorite activity' in Fig. 1 and 'announces what they want' is loose wording.

C4.1.note: Input format is not RANK/WEAK/APPR/DICH/PAIR, and voter utilities are not used in the main results.

C4.2.note: The term dichotomous preferences is not used.

C5.1.quote: egalitarian committee sequences ensure that each agent is satisfied
C5.1.note: The problem definitions require a minimum satisfaction per level and per agent (egalitarian/equitable), which is an evaluation by voter satisfaction criteria.

C5.2.note: Satisfaction is defined on the nominations with no statement relating them to held attitudes.

VOT.note: Agents only provide fixed nominations and take no action in the model.

ORG.note: The committee chooser is the solver of the computational problem, not an agent modelled with objectives.

claims.quote: short trips with few per-day activities like in our introductory example can be tractable
where egalitarian or even equitable solutions appear particularly relevant, can be solved efficiently

C9.2.quote: short trips with few per-day activities
C9.2.note: The claims about practical tractability and the relevance of egalitarian/equitable solutions need the assumption that nominations reflect agents' real satisfaction, and that agents report truthfully. Neither is stated.
